insider_note: This equation is neither homogeneous nor linear in y, so neither of the two standard methods applies directly — the whole answer depends on spotting that y − x, not y/x, is the combination worth naming t.

steps.label: Substitute t = y − x
steps.margin_note: One mark. Differentiating t = y − x relates dt/dx to dy/dx before substituting into the equation.
steps.memory_tip: t = y − x gives dt/dx = dy/dx − 1, so dy/dx = dt/dx + 1.
lines: Given D.E is dy/dx − x tan(y − x) = 1
Put y − x = t ⇒ dy/dx − 1 = dt/dx
steps.why: The awkward term tan(y − x) only makes sense as a function of the single combination y − x, so naming that combination t and rewriting dy/dx in terms of dt/dx removes the mixed x and y dependence.
common_mistakes: Writing dy/dx = dt/dx − 1 instead of dt/dx + 1, a sign slip from differentiating y − x = t.
Substituting t = x − y instead of y − x, inverting the sign of every later term.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. The equation becomes purely in t and x once the substitution is made.
steps.memory_tip: 1 cancels with 1 once dt/dx + 1 − x tan t = 1 is written out — the constant terms vanish first.
lines: the given D.E becomes (dt/dx + 1) − x tan t
⇒ dt/dx = x tan t ⇒ (1/tan t) dt = x dx
steps.why: Substituting the relation from step 1 into the original equation cancels the constant terms and leaves dt/dx = x tan t, which separates cleanly into a t-only side and an x-only side.
common_mistakes: Missing that the two 1's on either side of the equation cancel exactly.
Inverting tan t to cot t incorrectly, writing tan t dt = x dx instead of cot t dt = x dx.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: One mark. ∫cot t dt = log(sin t) is a standard integral.
steps.memory_tip: cot t = cos t/sin t, and the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator — a direct log form.
steps.why: cot t is cos t over sin t, and cos t is the derivative of sin t, so the left integral is the standard log(sin t); the right side is the plain power-rule integral of x.
common_mistakes: Integrating cot t as log(cos t) instead of log(sin t).
Forgetting the /2 that comes from integrating x on the right side.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Multiply by 2 and substitute t = y − x back in.
steps.memory_tip: Multiplying by 2 clears the /2 on the right and doubles the log on the left, matching the book's marked form.
steps.why: Multiplying the whole equation by 2 clears the fraction on the right, and substituting t = y − x back in returns the final relation to the original variables x and y, with the doubled constant of integration 2c relabelled as c.
common_mistakes: Assuming the boxed line must show 2c since the equation was multiplied by 2 — the doubled constant of integration is silently relabelled as c, a standard convenience since the constant is arbitrary either way, not a missed step.
Substituting t = x − y instead of y − x at this final stage.
